title: Berry v. Reagan — D.C. Circuit mootness disposition
lead: A dispute over removing Civil Rights Commissioners reaches appeal, but expiration of the Commission’s authorized existence leads to vacatur and mootness rather than a removal-power holding.

actors.name: President Ronald Reagan
actors.role: Appellant seeking reversal and a stay of the district judgment.

actors.name: Berry and the other appellees
actors.role: Parties opposing Reagan’s motion in the commissioner-removal litigation.

actors.name: Civil Rights Commission
actors.role: Body whose statutory period of existence as constituted expired while the case was pending.

proceedings: The assigned account reports a district preliminary injunction against removals.
After appellate argument, the D.C.Circuit vacated and remanded for dismissal as moot.
The appellate order was later ordered published; the district opinion remains a separate source gap.
limits: The appellate order does not adjudicate presidential removal power. The district injunction’s complete text is unavailable. Textbook accounts of political compromise and Commission restructuring are historical context, not findings in this short appellate order.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Reagan’s removal of commissioners prompts district relief
sections.cue: Which stage does the available appellate order follow?
paragraphs: The assigned account describes President Reagan removing three Civil Rights Commissioners in 1983 and a district court entering a preliminary injunction blocking the removals. That district decision is a separate stage, identified in later judicial citations as a November 14, 1983 ruling; its complete text is unavailable here.
Reagan appealed and requested summary reversal and a stay pending appeal. Berry and the other appellees opposed the motion, and Reagan replied. The D.C.Circuit heard oral argument on November 21.

sources.pinpoint: Assigned controversy and appellate posture;732 F.2d 949; assigned 190–191

sections.title: Statutory expiration changes the controversy before the appeal is decided
sections.cue: What intervening circumstance supplied the ground for decision?
paragraphs: Before granting or denying the requested appellate relief on its merits, the panel confronted expiration of the authorized period for the Commission’s existence as then constituted under 42 U.S.C. § 1975c(d).

The order treated that statutory expiration as eliminating the live controversy in this suit. It did not reconstruct the commissioners’ appointments, removal letters or district evidentiary findings, and it did not need to decide which side was right about presidential removal authority.

sections.title: The panel vacates and orders dismissal rather than deciding removal power
sections.cue: What happened to the district judgment?
paragraphs: On November 30, 1983, a unanimous per curiam panel of Judges Wilkey, Mikva and Senior Judge McGowan vacated the district judgment and remanded with instructions to dismiss the suit as moot. It relied on the mootness-vacatur authorities United States v. Munsingwear and Great Western Sugar Co. v. Nelson, and directed the clerk to transmit a certified copy to the district court.

Vacatur removed the district judgment; it neither affirmed its removal-power reasoning nor rejected that reasoning on the merits. The panel also referred to its recent tenure-of-office decision, Kalaris v. Donovan, but expressly declined to reaffirm any of its teachings here.

sources.pinpoint: Mootness reasoning and operative order;732 F.2d 949

sections.title: Later publication does not enlarge the narrow appellate result
sections.cue: How does the assigned political history relate to the order?
paragraphs: The appellate order was directed to be published on March 20, 1984. It contained no judicial footnotes, dissent or separate writing.

The textbook also describes a political compromise retaining two commissioners and legislation expanding membership from six to eight and making the Commission independent. That historical account supplies context for the dispute. The reported appellate judgment itself rests on statutory expiration and mootness, not a decision that an executive-agency label resolves commissioners’ tenure.
